title: AD Replication Internals: Topology, USNs, and Lingering Objects
summary: How the KCC builds topology, how up-to-dateness vectors and USNs drive convergence, and why lingering objects are dangerous.
architecture_notes: The KCC runs on every DC and independently computes an intrasite ring topology (and, with the Inter-Site Topology Generator, intersite links) so any DC can reach any other within a bounded number of hops. Intrasite replication is notify-driven (near-immediate after a change); intersite replication is schedule-driven, which trades convergence latency for WAN bandwidth control.
internals: Each object attribute carries a Update Sequence Number (USN) local to its originating DC; a destination DC tracks the highest USN it has already received per source DC (its up-to-dateness vector) so replication is idempotent and doesn't resend what's already applied. Deletions become tombstones held for the tombstone lifetime (default 180 days on modern forests) so replication has time to converge before the object is fully garbage-collected.
failure_modes: A DC offline longer than the tombstone lifetime can no longer replicate a deletion correctly - a deleted object can resurface as a lingering object on that DC and then re-propagate if strict replication consistency isn't enforced (Event IDs 1388/1988/2042). Topology mismatches (Event 1311) happen when the AD DS site/subnet configuration doesn't reflect the real WAN topology, causing the KCC to build unreachable or inefficient links.
trade_offs: Strict replication consistency (the default since Windows Server 2003 SP1) blocks a lingering object from being written back in, at the cost of that DC refusing to replicate the affected partition until manually remediated - a deliberate fail-safe, not a bug.
enterprise_design_notes: Design sites and subnets to mirror physical WAN topology exactly; under-provisioning intersite replication schedules on high-change environments is a common self-inflicted cause of tombstone-lifetime replication failures.

title: FSMO Internals: Why Single-Master Exists At All
summary: The conflict classes FSMO roles exist to prevent, and why 'last writer wins' isn't good enough for them.
architecture_notes: AD DS is multi-master and resolves most conflicting concurrent writes with a 'last writer wins' rule on a per-attribute basis. FSMO roles exist specifically for the handful of operations where last-writer-wins would produce an inconsistent or unsafe result forest- or domain-wide.
internals: RID Master hands out blocks of Relative IDs to every DC in the domain; a DC creates new security principals from its local RID pool without contacting the RID Master on every object creation - only when its pool is exhausted. Schema Master gates the schema naming context so two DCs can never apply conflicting, unmergeable schema extensions simultaneously (e.g. two products both claiming the same new attribute OID).
failure_modes: Seizing a role and later reconnecting the original, unaware holder to the network is the classic self-inflicted incident: you now have two DCs both believing they hold the same single-master role, defeating the entire purpose of FSMO.
trade_offs: Concentrating all five roles on one DC simplifies tracking but creates a single dependency point for schema changes, new security principal creation, and PDC-dependent functions; spreading them out adds resilience but adds operational tracking overhead.
enterprise_design_notes: Always designate and document a standby role holder (a direct intrasite replication partner) per role so a seize decision under pressure has a pre-agreed target, not an improvised one.

title: Forest Recovery Internals: Why Order and Isolation Matter
summary: Why the first recovered DC must be isolated and why authoritative SYSVOL restore happens exactly once.
architecture_notes: Recovery restores exactly one writable DC per domain from a trusted backup, root domain first (it holds Schema Admins/Enterprise Admins and typically the forest DNS root), then works down the domain hierarchy so trust and DNS delegation are never rebuilt out of order.
internals: The first recovered DC in each domain gets a nonauthoritative AD DS restore plus an authoritative SYSVOL restore (DFSR) - authoritative exactly once, because every other DC that later resynchronizes SYSVOL treats this copy as ground truth; running an authoritative SYSVOL restore on more than one DC creates conflicting 'ground truths' and DFSR replication conflicts. Network isolation before restore prevents a corrupted or compromised live topology from immediately re-infecting or out-of-band replicating over the freshly restored DC before it's verified clean.
failure_modes: Skipping isolation and joining the restored DC straight to production risks replicating the very corruption or compromise you were recovering from, right back onto the new baseline. Restoring an operations-master-holding DC without the documented registry workaround for initial synchronization can leave AD DS unavailable until full replication convergence, extending the outage.
trade_offs: Choosing an older, more conservative backup reduces the risk of restoring already-corrupted data but increases the amount of legitimate recent work that is lost; there is no restore point that avoids this trade-off.
enterprise_design_notes: The Microsoft forest recovery guide as retrieved explicitly targets DCs on Windows Server 2012 through 2022; for Windows Server 2025 estates, validate against the 2025-specific edition of the guide before treating any 2025-only behavior as confirmed - flagged here as VERSION_CURRENT_WITH_CONTEXT rather than asserted.

title: Kerberos Internals: Delegation Types and Why RBCD Won Out
summary: Unconstrained vs constrained vs resource-based constrained delegation, and the security reasoning behind Microsoft's current recommendation.
architecture_notes: Delegation lets a front-end service present a user's identity to a back-end service on the user's behalf. Three mechanisms exist: unconstrained (front-end can impersonate the user to any service anywhere - broad blast radius), constrained (front-end may only impersonate to a specific, pre-declared list of services, same-domain only), and resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD, configured on the back-end resource itself, works across domains and even across trusted forests).
internals: With RBCD, the back-end service's account carries the ACL of which front-end accounts may delegate to it (msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity), inverting control from the front-end/domain admin to the resource owner - which is why it supports cross-forest scenarios that constrained delegation explicitly does not.
failure_modes: Unconstrained delegation is 'supported but not recommended' in every topology Microsoft documents, because a compromised front-end service holding unconstrained delegation rights can impersonate any user to any service in the forest - a well-known Kerberos privilege-escalation path in real incidents.
trade_offs: Constrained delegation is simpler to reason about but breaks at domain boundaries; RBCD is more flexible and crosses trust boundaries but requires the resource owner (not just the front-end's domain admin) to correctly maintain the allow-list.
enterprise_design_notes: Treat any discovered unconstrained delegation grant as a finding to remediate, not a configuration to leave alone - migrate to constrained delegation or RBCD as the service topology allows.

title: gMSA Internals: The Key Distribution Service and Why Clustering Is the Exception
summary: How the KDS root key drives gMSA password computation, and why the Cluster service specifically doesn't support gMSA directly.
architecture_notes: The Microsoft Key Distribution Service (kdssvc.dll) on a DC holds a shared secret (the KDS root key, created once per forest) from which it derives per-account keys. A domain controller computes the current gMSA password from that key plus the account's attributes; any authorized member host retrieves the current (and immediately preceding, for rollover safety) password value via LDAP.
internals: Because password computation is deterministic from the KDS root key plus time, every authorized host independently arrives at the same current password without a central password-push mechanism - this is what lets a server farm of arbitrary size share one identity without password-sync tooling.
failure_modes: A gMSA host that isn't on the account's authorized-principals list simply cannot retrieve the password (fails closed, not open) - the common operational mistake is forgetting to add a newly-added farm member to that list. Encryption-type mismatches matter here too: if a host is configured to reject RC4 and the gMSA account's msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute isn't set for AES, authentication fails outright.
trade_offs: gMSA removes password-rotation operational burden entirely but requires domain functional level 2012+ and depends on DC availability for password retrieval - an isolated host that can't reach any DC can't refresh its cached password past expiry.
enterprise_design_notes: Failover clustering is the specific, named exception: the Cluster service itself doesn't support gMSA, though services running on top of it (a Windows service, an IIS app pool, a scheduled task) can still use one if they natively support gMSA/sMSA - don't conflate 'runs on a cluster node' with 'the Cluster service supports it'.
